title: Recipe Scaler: Double, Halve or Resize Any Recipe
excerpt: Paste an ingredient list, enter the servings you need and get every amount scaled, in fractions, with tips on eggs, pan sizes and baking times.
html:
Cooking for two from a recipe that feeds six, or doubling a favourite for a crowd? Paste the ingredients below, set the servings, and every amount is recalculated and written as a kitchen-friendly fraction.

How it works: divide the servings you need by the servings the recipe makes, then multiply every amount by that number. Going from 4 servings to 6 means multiplying by 1½.

Recipe scaler

Paste one ingredient per line, exactly as the recipe writes it. Amounts like 2, 1½, 1 1/2, ¾ and 2-3 are all understood.

How to scale a recipe by hand

To makeMultiply every amount by
Half the recipe0.5
One and a half times1.5
Twice as much2
Three times as much3
4 servings from a recipe for 6⅔ (4 ÷ 6)
10 servings from a recipe for 42½ (10 ÷ 4)

Halving awkward amounts

Recipe saysHalf is
1 cup½ cup
¾ cup6 tablespoons
⅓ cup2 tablespoons + 2 teaspoons
¼ cup2 tablespoons
1 tablespoon1½ teaspoons
1 teaspoon½ teaspoon
1 large eggAbout 1½ tablespoons of beaten egg

What doesn't scale in a straight line

  • Eggs. Round to whole eggs where you can. For half an egg, beat one and measure out half: a large egg is about 3 tablespoons.
  • Pan size. A doubled batter needs twice the pan area, not a deeper pan. An 8-inch square pan holds 64 square inches; a 9×13 pan holds 117, close to two of them.
  • Baking time and temperature. Keep the oven temperature the same and start checking at the original time; a bigger or deeper pan takes longer.
  • Salt, spices and leaveners. When tripling or more, add a little less than the maths says, then taste and adjust.
  • Cooking on the stove. A doubled pot of soup takes longer to come to a boil, and a crowded pan steams instead of browning, so cook in batches.

Recipe scaling FAQ

How do I double a recipe?

Multiply every ingredient amount by 2, keep the oven temperature the same, use a pan twice the size (or two pans), and check for doneness from the original time.

How do I cut a recipe in half?

Multiply every amount by 0.5. Use the table above for awkward amounts like ⅓ cup and one egg.

Do I double the baking time when I double a recipe?

No. In two pans the time stays about the same; in one larger, deeper pan it takes longer, but rarely twice as long. Check early and often.

Can I scale baking recipes?

Yes, but weigh ingredients if you can: grams scale exactly, while cups and spoons add up rounding errors. The cups to grams converter helps.
